title: Landscape
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on paper

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, John Stewart Kennedy Fund, 1913
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A section of a long handscroll showing a mountain landscape painted in ink and soft color on paper. Rocky peaks rise above the scenery in detailed, layered brushwork.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, period, tags (Mountains, Landscapes), public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record. The record gives no description of the scenes, so the text stays at the level of mountains and landscape.

context: A handscroll landscape dated 1558 by Wen Boren, a Ming dynasty painter who is generally known as a member of the Wen family of artists of Suzhou. It is painted in ink and color on paper. Handscrolls are unrolled gradually, so a landscape unfolds like a journey.

descriptions.k: This is a long painting of mountains. You look at it a little at a time as it unrolls. The painter used ink and soft color. Where would you walk if you could go inside?
descriptions.g12: Wen Boren painted these mountains on a long scroll in China, more than 450 years ago. People unrolled it slowly, like turning pages. He used ink and soft color. As you look, imagine you are on a trip through the landscape. Where would you stop to rest?
descriptions.g35: A handscroll is a long painting that you unroll a little at a time, so the view changes like a journey. Wen Boren painted this mountain landscape in 1558 with ink and color on paper. Look for how the peaks and scenery are layered. Why might a painter make a picture that unfolds slowly instead of one you see all at once?
descriptions.g68: Handscrolls were viewed in sections, from right to left, held in the viewer's hands, which turns looking into a slow journey. Wen Boren, a painter of the Wen family of Suzhou, dated this mountain landscape 1558. Ink and color on paper create layered peaks and scenery. How does a painting that unrolls change your sense of time and space compared with one that hangs?
descriptions.g910: The handscroll format shapes how this 1558 landscape is experienced: viewers reveal one section at a time, so composition unfolds in sequence rather than all at once. Wen Boren, linked to the Suzhou painting circle of the Wen family, uses ink and color to build mountains and scenery. Consider how pacing, transitions between sections, and the contrast of dense and open passages might guide a viewer on an imagined journey.
descriptions.g1112: A handscroll landscape complicates the notion of a single viewpoint: the composition exists as a sequence, experienced by hands and time. Wen Boren's 1558 scroll belongs to the Suzhou tradition associated with his family, in which landscape often served as a vehicle for cultivated reflection. The record gives little detail on the scenery, so interpretation should proceed from what is visible in each section. How does the scroll format shape both seeing and meaning?

k.daily: Look at the tallest mountain in this long painting. What do you think is behind it?
k.emotion: Does this landscape feel calm or exciting? What do you see that tells you?
k.observation: Find a mountain, a tree, and a bit of empty space. Point to each.
k.analysis: Where in this long picture do your eyes want to start? Why?
k.line: Trace the edge of a mountain with your finger. Does it go up, down, or zigzag?
k.shape: The mountains are big shapes. Do they look pointy, round, or lumpy?
k.color: What soft colors do you see along with the black ink?
k.texture: Do the mountains look smooth or rough? Which marks make them look that way?
k.space: What is close to you in the scroll? What looks far away?
k.light: Does the scene look sunny, misty, or cloudy? What clue shows you?
k.meaning: If you were walking through this scroll, what would you want to find?
k.culture: This painting is a long scroll that people unrolled slowly. Why might that be a nice way to look at mountains?
k.technique: The painter used a brush with ink and color on paper. Where do you think he used a very thin line?
k.personal: What is the biggest hill or mountain you have seen? How did it feel to look at it?
k.critical: How is looking at a long scroll different from looking at a photograph?

g12.daily: Imagine walking through this landscape from one edge to the other. What would you see first and last?
g12.emotion: What feeling does this mountain scene give you, quiet, strong, or mysterious? What helps you decide?
g12.observation: Name five things you can find among the peaks and scenery of Wen Boren's scroll.
g12.analysis: How does the painter layer mountains so that some look near and others look far?
g12.line: Compare the lines for the mountain edges with the lines for the trees. How do they differ?
g12.shape: Look at the big mountain shapes and the small shapes around them. How do they fit together?
g12.color: The painter used ink and soft color. Where does the color help the picture most?
g12.texture: How does the painter show rocky surfaces on the mountains?
g12.space: Where does the picture feel crowded, and where does it feel open?
g12.light: How does the painter make some parts look bright and others look shaded?
g12.meaning: Why do you think people liked paintings of mountains and nature?
g12.culture: People unrolled a scroll like this in their hands, a little at a time. How is that different from seeing a picture on a wall?
g12.technique: Wen Boren made a very long painting. What would be hard about keeping the style the same all the way along?
g12.personal: If you could make a long picture of your own neighborhood, what would it show?
g12.critical: Do you think a long scroll tells a story even without people in it? Explain.

g35.daily: How does this section of the scroll make you feel as if you are traveling through mountains?
g35.emotion: What mood does the mountain landscape set? Which details of shape, color, or space create it?
g35.observation: Look slowly from one edge to the other. What details do you notice only on a second pass?
g35.analysis: How does Wen Boren use the arrangement of mountains and scenery to move your eyes across the scroll?
g35.line: How do outlines and texture strokes work together to make mountains look solid?
g35.shape: How do repeated mountain shapes make a rhythm, and where does the painter change the pattern?
g35.color: How does soft color add to the ink lines without covering them?
g35.texture: How does the painter show the rough surface of rock using small brush marks?
g35.space: How does the painter suggest distance on a flat piece of paper?
g35.light: How can you tell from the painting whether the day is bright or gloomy?
g35.meaning: A landscape can be an image of a real place or an imagined one. What clues might help you decide for this scroll?
g35.culture: Wen Boren belonged to a family of Ming painters in Suzhou. What might this suggest about how artists learned and worked?
g35.technique: A handscroll is unrolled and rerolled many times. How might the painter plan a picture that is viewed in sections?
g35.personal: Think about a journey you remember. How could you show it as a long, unrolling picture?
g35.critical: The record only calls this painting Landscape. What would you want a title to say?

g68.daily: How does the handscroll format turn a mountain landscape into an experience over time?
g68.emotion: How do changes in the density of mountains and open space shift the emotional rhythm of the scene?
g68.observation: Describe how the scene changes from one side of the visible section to the other. What stays constant?
g68.analysis: How does the composition use mountain masses and open areas to pace the viewer's eye?
g68.line: Where do firm contour lines and softer texture strokes meet, and how do they create the feel of solid rock?
g68.shape: How do the vertical mountain shapes interact with the horizontal format of the scroll?
g68.color: How does the limited use of color keep the scroll unified while adding interest?
g68.texture: Which brush techniques stand out for rocks, trees, and ground? How do they differ?
g68.space: How does the painter move from foreground to distance without using a single fixed viewpoint?
g68.light: How does tonal variation suggest atmosphere in the mountains without strong shadows?
g68.meaning: How might a scholar have seen a mountain landscape as a place for reflection or imagined travel?
g68.culture: The Wen family was admired in Suzhou for painting and calligraphy. How might family tradition have shaped the style of this scroll?
g68.technique: Wen Boren painted in ink and color on paper, a material that absorbs quickly. How does that affect the confidence needed in brushwork?
g68.personal: How would you show the feeling of a long walk in a single painting?
g68.critical: What do we lose and gain when a handscroll is shown as a single image on a screen?

g910.daily: Which formal features of this section best show how the scroll format shapes composition?
g910.emotion: How does the interplay of dense mountain forms and open passages produce an emotional pace across the scroll?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy within the section. What draws attention first, and what devices cause that?
g910.analysis: Analyze how the mountains, trees, and open areas are sequenced to guide a viewer through the scroll.
g910.line: How do contour and texture strokes together create structure, and where does line become expressive?
g910.shape: How do vertical forms of peaks create counterpoint to the horizontal movement of the handscroll?
g910.color: How does the restrained use of color support atmosphere and unity along the scroll?
g910.texture: How does the layering of texture strokes produce the impression of weight and surface?
g910.space: How does the scroll construct deep space through overlap, scale, and tone rather than a single vanishing point?
g910.light: How is a convincing sense of atmosphere established through tonal contrast alone?
g910.meaning: How might this landscape function as an image of retreat, journey, or cultivated taste, and what evidence supports each idea?
g910.culture: How does a Suzhou family of painters help explain the role of landscape in educated Ming society?
g910.technique: What do ink and color on paper demand of a painter working on a long scroll?
g910.personal: How does the experience of controlling the pace of looking change your relationship with an artwork?
g910.critical: How limited is our reading when we see only one section of a scroll? What would you most want to see next?

g1112.daily: What can the section of the scroll shown here support about Wen Boren's approach, and what requires the full scroll?
g1112.emotion: How does the temporal unfolding of a handscroll complicate the attribution of a single mood to the work?
g1112.observation: Describe the scroll's visible section precisely. When does description turn into interpretation?
g1112.analysis: Analyze the relationship between sequence and composition in a format that is never seen all at once.
g1112.line: How do the conventions of contour and texture strokes link this scroll to a longer landscape tradition, and where might the individual hand be visible?
g1112.shape: How do mountain masses articulate rhythm and pacing along the horizontal axis?
g1112.color: How does modest color function in relation to ink structure, and how might age have altered its appearance?
g1112.texture: How do accumulated brush marks both describe and abstract the substance of rock?
g1112.space: How does shifting perspective across the scroll offer an alternative to single-point perspective, and what does it imply about viewing?
g1112.light: How does the painting evoke atmosphere through tonal gradation, and how does that compare with other traditions of landscape?
g1112.meaning: How do readings of landscape as a real place, an imagined retreat, or a scholar's cultivated emblem differ, and what limits our certainty here?
g1112.culture: How does the Wen family's standing in Suzhou shape interpretations of this scroll as a work of cultivated amateur taste or professional skill?
g1112.technique: How does the scroll format affect the order, speed, and risk of painting decisions?
g1112.personal: How does your own experience of travel or place shape how you move through an imagined landscape?
g1112.critical: How should viewers weigh the generic title Landscape against the specific visual evidence when interpreting a work?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium, period and tags (Mountains, Landscapes) in the Met record were checked; the subject is a mountain landscape.

teacherNote.context: Dated 1558, this handscroll is by Wen Boren, of the Suzhou painting family. The record gives no scene description, so ground discussion in what students see in the image.
directions: Have students tape paper into a long strip and draw a journey that changes from left to right.
Discuss how viewing a long scroll in sections differs from seeing a photo all at once.
Ask students to give the scroll a descriptive title and justify it.
